blocks.text: Stepping from a hot sauna into cold water imposes opposite heat loads within a minute, yet core temperature stays within about a degree of 37 degrees Celsius. A small region at the base of the brain is comparing a measured temperature with a target and adjusting blood flow, sweat glands and muscles to close the gap, and the same circuit can have its target moved upward by infection.

blocks.markdown: **Core temperature and why it matters.** Humans are **homeotherms**: core temperature is held near **37 degrees Celsius** (usual range about 36.5-37.5), varying by about 0.5 degrees through the day (lowest in the early morning, highest in the late afternoon) and rising by a few tenths of a degree after ovulation. Enzymes, ion channels and membrane properties work best in a narrow range, so a rise of a few degrees or a fall of several degrees quickly disturbs function. Temperature is regulated as a balance: **heat gained** (from metabolism and from the environment) equals **heat lost**.

blocks.title: Core temperature and set point
blocks.text: Core temperature is the temperature of the deep tissues of the head and trunk (measured, for example, in the oesophagus, rectum or tympanic membrane); skin temperature is lower and variable. The set point is the target temperature, about 37 degrees Celsius, against which the hypothalamus compares input from temperature sensors; a deviation triggers effector responses.

blocks.markdown:
**Heat production.** Heat is a by-product of metabolism, so every tissue contributes.

- **Basal metabolism:** the largest source at rest, especially liver, heart, brain and muscle.
- **Skeletal muscle:** exercise can multiply heat production many times, and **shivering** (involuntary rhythmic contraction) raises it up to several-fold.
- **Non-shivering thermogenesis:** sympathetic and thyroid hormone stimulation of metabolism; **brown adipose tissue**, rich in the uncoupling protein UCP1 that makes heat instead of ATP, is important in infants.
- **Diet-induced thermogenesis:** the rise in heat after eating.
- **Hormones:** thyroid hormones set basal heat production; adrenaline increases it acutely.

**Routes of heat loss.** Heat moves from the core to the skin by conduction and by blood flow, then leaves the skin by four mechanisms.

- **Radiation:** infrared emission; the main route at rest in a comfortable environment (roughly half or more).
- **Conduction:** direct transfer to a cooler object in contact (for example cold water, which conducts heat about 25 times faster than air).
- **Convection:** heat carried away by moving air or water; wind and fans increase it.
- **Evaporation:** vaporisation of water from the skin and airways; about 2.4 kJ is absorbed per gram of water evaporated. Insensible loss occurs continuously, and **sweating** adds to it.

When environmental temperature rises above skin temperature, radiation, conduction and convection add heat to the body, so **evaporation becomes the only way to lose heat**. High humidity limits evaporation, which is why humid heat is dangerous.

blocks.caption: Change in body temperature (degrees C) from net stored heat Q (kJ), body mass m (kg) and specific heat capacity c of tissue, about 3.5 kJ per kg per degree C.

blocks.title: How fast does stored heat raise temperature?
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg adult stores a net 490 kJ of heat (heat production exceeding heat loss). Using c = 3.5 kJ/kg/degree C, what is the rise in mean body temperature?

steps.text: Calculate the heat needed to raise the body by one degree.
Divide the stored heat by this value.
Interpret: a net imbalance of only a few hundred kilojoules raises temperature by 2 degrees, so the effector systems must respond within minutes.

blocks.answer: The mean body temperature rises by 2.0 degrees C.

blocks.markdown:
**The hypothalamic thermostat.** Two sets of sensors feed the hypothalamus. **Peripheral thermoreceptors** in the skin (separate warm and cold receptors, with cold receptors more numerous) provide early warning of environmental change. **Central thermoreceptors** in the **preoptic area and anterior hypothalamus**, spinal cord and viscera detect core temperature. The **anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area)** is chiefly concerned with **heat loss**, and the **posterior hypothalamus** integrates inputs and drives **heat conservation and production**; the integrated output adjusts effectors.

**Responses to cold:** cutaneous **vasoconstriction** (increased sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone, reducing skin blood flow and heat loss), **shivering** (via descending motor pathways), non-shivering thermogenesis (sympathetic and thyroid activity), **piloerection** (of little value in humans), curling up and behaviour such as putting on clothes.

**Responses to heat:** cutaneous **vasodilation** (reduced sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone, increasing skin blood flow and heat loss), **sweating** (sympathetic cholinergic nerves releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors of eccrine sweat glands), reduced muscle activity and behaviour such as seeking shade and removing clothes.

blocks.caption: Effector responses of the hypothalamic thermostat.
rows: Seek warmth, add clothing, curl up
Reduced voluntary activity and heat production

blocks.title: Sweat required to dissipate exercise heat
blocks.prompt: During a long run, a runner must dissipate 600 W (600 J per second) by evaporation. Taking the heat absorbed as 2.43 kJ per gram of water evaporated, how many grams of sweat must evaporate per hour?

steps.text: Convert power to energy per hour.
Divide by the heat absorbed per gram.
Interpret: about 0.9 L per hour must evaporate, and sweat that drips off without evaporating does not cool the body.

blocks.answer: About 890 g (0.89 L) of sweat must evaporate per hour.

blocks.markdown: **Fever: pyrogens reset the set point.** A **pyrogen** is a substance that causes fever. **Exogenous pyrogens**, such as lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria, stimulate macrophages and other cells to release **endogenous pyrogens**, the cytokines **interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor-alpha**. These act at the **organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT)**, a region lacking the usual blood-brain barrier, and induce **cyclo-oxygenase-2** and production of **prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)** in the preoptic hypothalamus. PGE2 **raises the set point**. The body now regards its normal temperature as too cold, so it conserves and produces heat (vasoconstriction, shivering, 'chills' or rigors) until the core reaches the new higher set point. When the pyrogen stimulus ends, or an antipyretic is taken, the set point returns toward normal; the body now senses it is too hot and sweats and vasodilates (the fever 'breaks'). **Antipyretics** such as aspirin and paracetamol act by reducing prostaglandin synthesis (pharmacology teaching example). Fever therefore results from a **regulated** rise in set point, not a failure of regulation.

items: Heat production: basal metabolism, muscle activity and shivering, brown fat and thyroid or adrenaline-driven thermogenesis, digestion.
Heat loss: radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation; only evaporation works when the environment is hotter than skin.
Cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, thermogenesis; heat: vasodilation and sweating.
Pyrogens raise the set point through cytokines and PGE2; the body then behaves as though it is cold until the new set point is reached.

blocks.title: Set point versus temperature
blocks.text: A fever means the set point has risen and effectors drive temperature to match it. During the rise the patient feels cold and shivers even though the thermometer reads high. When the set point falls, the same effectors work in reverse to lose heat. Keep this idea of a moving target; it is what distinguishes fever from other raised temperatures.

blocks.title: Sweating is cholinergic, vasoconstriction is adrenergic
blocks.text: Eccrine sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic nerves that release acetylcholine, a common exam trap, whereas cutaneous vasoconstriction uses noradrenaline on alpha-1 receptors. Also, evaporation of sweat cools only if sweat actually evaporates; in very humid air it does not.

points: Core temperature is held near 37 degrees Celsius by balancing heat production (metabolism, muscle, thermogenesis) against heat loss (radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation).
The hypothalamus integrates central and skin thermoreceptor input and compares it with a set point, then drives vasomotor, sweating, shivering and behavioural effectors.

Cold causes cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering and thermogenesis; heat causes vasodilation and cholinergic sweating; evaporation is the only route of loss when the environment is hotter than the skin.
Exogenous pyrogens trigger IL-1, IL-6 and TNF release, which raise PGE2 in the preoptic hypothalamus and reset the set point upward, producing fever.

questions.stem: Which structure is the main integrating centre for body temperature regulation?

options.text: The hypothalamus (preoptic area and posterior hypothalamus)

questions.correctOptionText: The hypothalamus (preoptic area and posterior hypothalamus)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it receives central and peripheral temperature input and drives effectors.
distractorRationale.b: The cerebellum coordinates movement and is not the thermostat.
distractorRationale.c: The adrenal cortex is an endocrine gland, not an integrating centre.

questions.explanation: The preoptic area and anterior hypothalamus sense core temperature and the posterior hypothalamus integrates inputs to produce responses. It compares the measured temperature with the set point and activates the appropriate effectors.

questions.stem: In a desert with an air temperature of 45 degrees Celsius, which route of heat loss is available to a person whose skin temperature is 35 degrees Celsius?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: evaporation absorbs heat regardless of the environmental temperature (if humidity allows).
distractorRationale.b: Radiation would add heat when the surroundings are hotter than the skin.
distractorRationale.c: Conduction to hotter air would add heat.
distractorRationale.d: Convection of hot air would add heat.

questions.explanation: When the environment is hotter than the skin, radiation, conduction and convection transfer heat into the body. Only evaporation, which uses heat to vaporise water, still removes heat, and it is limited by humidity.

questions.stem: Which pair of responses occurs when core temperature falls below the set point?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: heat is conserved by reducing skin blood flow and generated by shivering.
distractorRationale.c: Sweating loses heat and is not a response to cold.
distractorRationale.d: Vasodilation would increase heat loss in the cold.

questions.explanation: Cold activates sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow to the skin, reducing heat loss, and drives shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis to increase heat production. Both are coordinated by the hypothalamus.

questions.stem: Which statement about eccrine sweating is correct?

options.text: It is mediated by sympathetic cholinergic nerves acting on muscarinic receptors
It is mediated by parasympathetic nerves acting on nicotinic receptors
It is mediated by sympathetic noradrenergic nerves acting on alpha-1 receptors
It is triggered only by circulating adrenaline

questions.correctOptionText: It is mediated by sympathetic cholinergic nerves acting on muscarinic receptors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the exception where sympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine.
distractorRationale.c: Alpha-1 stimulation causes vasoconstriction, not sweating.
distractorRationale.d: Circulating adrenaline is not the main trigger.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic postganglionic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors. This is why anticholinergic drugs reduce sweating and can raise the risk of overheating.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a bacterial throat infection has a temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius and is shivering, with pale cool skin, while rising. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Prostaglandin E2 has raised the hypothalamic set point, so he is cold relative to the new target
His heat loss mechanisms have failed at a normal set point
Bacterial toxins directly paralyse sweat glands, causing the fever
The set point has fallen below core temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Prostaglandin E2 has raised the hypothalamic set point, so he is cold relative to the new target

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vasoconstriction and shivering raise temperature to the new set point.
distractorRationale.b: Fever is not failure of regulation; the set point is changed.
distractorRationale.c: Bacterial products act through cytokines and PGE2 on the hypothalamus.
distractorRationale.d: A lowered set point would cause sweating and vasodilation.

questions.explanation: Cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) induce PGE2 in the preoptic hypothalamus, raising the set point. The body is then below its target, so it conserves heat by vasoconstriction (pale, cool skin) and generates heat by shivering until temperature matches the new set point.

questions.stem: Antipyretics such as aspirin and paracetamol lower fever by reducing the synthesis of prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus.
questions.explanation: These drugs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and so reduce PGE2 production, which allows the set point to return towards normal. They do not lower the temperature of a person with a normal set point.

questions.stem: An 80 kg man exercising in a warm room produces heat at a net rate of 400 W but loses heat at 340 W. Assume the net heat is stored uniformly and that tissue specific heat is 3.5 kJ per kg per degree C. By how many degrees Celsius does his mean body temperature rise in one hour?
questions.explanation: The net rate of heat gain is 400 - 340 = 60 W = 60 J/s, so in 3600 s he stores 216,000 J = 216 kJ. Heat capacity is 80 x 3.5 = 280 kJ per degree C, so the rise is 216/280 = 0.77 degrees C. A small mismatch between production and loss therefore produces a significant temperature rise over an hour.

questions.stem: A cyclist must dissipate 900 W by evaporation of sweat. If 2.43 kJ of heat is absorbed per gram of water evaporated, what mass of sweat, in grams per hour, must evaporate?
questions.explanation: 900 W x 3600 s = 3,240,000 J = 3240 kJ per hour. Dividing by 2.43 kJ/g gives about 1333 g/h, or roughly 1.3 L of sweat per hour that must actually evaporate. This explains why dehydration and high humidity limit exercise in the heat.

questions.stem: List the sources of heat production and the routes of heat loss, and explain how the hypothalamus coordinates the responses to a cold environment and a hot environment.
markingGuide: Heat production: basal metabolism, skeletal muscle activity and shivering, non-shivering thermogenesis (brown fat, thyroid hormone, adrenaline), diet-induced thermogenesis
Heat loss: radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation (insensible loss and sweat)
Evaporation is the only route when the environment is hotter than skin
Peripheral (skin) and central (preoptic/anterior hypothalamus, spinal cord, viscera) thermoreceptors feed the hypothalamus, which compares temperature with the set point
Cold: cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering, non-shivering thermogenesis and behaviour
Heat: cutaneous vasodilation, sweating (sympathetic cholinergic), reduced activity and behaviour
questions.explanation: Temperature regulation is a feedback system in which sensors, an integrator and effectors act to hold core temperature at the set point. Matching each response to its direction of change shows how the system works.

questions.stem: Explain how pyrogens cause fever, including the sequence of mediators, why the patient shivers during the rising phase, and what happens when the fever resolves.
markingGuide: Exogenous pyrogens (for example bacterial lipopolysaccharide) stimulate macrophages to release endogenous pyrogens: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha
Cytokines act on the OVLT/preoptic hypothalamus and induce cyclo-oxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E2 production
PGE2 raises the hypothalamic set point
Core temperature is now below the new set point, so the body conserves heat (vasoconstriction, pale skin) and produces heat (shivering, rigors) until the new set point is reached
When the pyrogen stimulus declines or an antipyretic inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, the set point falls
The body is now too hot relative to the set point, so vasodilation and sweating occur and temperature falls
Fever is a regulated rise in set point, not failure of thermoregulation
questions.explanation: Fever is an orderly resetting of the thermostat. The chills of the rising phase and the sweats of the falling phase are the effectors behaving normally relative to a moving target.
